kaigo-atomic-risk-observation.heading: Observe risks and share near misses
paragraphs: In observation, distinguish words and actions learned through interaction from actually measured information such as temperature and blood pressure. Noticing a change from usual does not establish its cause. Do not record feeling warmth by touch as a temperature measurement.

Loose footwear, long hems, wet floors, route cables and faulty equipment create different risks. An action possible yesterday may be difficult with today’s condition. Consider risks not only in walking but in moving while seated or lying and in transfers between a bed and equipment. Age or disability names alone do not determine one uniform judgment.

Risk management means anticipating hazards and preparing to prevent accidents. Record and share near misses even when no injury occurs. Separate the situation and event, confirmed factors and unconfirmed causes, then review responses and recurrence prevention as a team. Do not wait for harm before learning.

[Different learning example] A wheelchair moved before a transfer. If inspection confirms that the brakes were not applied, record that fact and share a checking method for the next task. If the cause has not been investigated, do not first declare the brakes responsible; report the movement and what remains to be checked.

Kenko means health generally, taicho means physical condition at a particular time, and kaoiro means facial coloring or appearance. Vital signs include temperature, breathing, pulse and blood pressure as indicators of life and condition. Seeing facial color differs from measuring a value, just as planned measurement differs from completed measurement.

Hakike means feeling like vomiting; oto means actually vomiting. Hakkan means sweating; hatsunetsu means temperature higher than usual. A picture of wiping sweat gives no temperature value. Hareru means swelling, while mukumu refers to edema; in reports, specify the site and change.

Contracture means restricted joint movement, not temporarily tensing a muscle. Pressure injuries involve skin or tissue damage related to pressure and can occur beyond people confined to bed. Heat illness and heat shock associated with sudden temperature changes, such as during bathing, are not identical terms. Learn the vocabulary here without independently deciding diagnoses or procedures.

Itai means pain; kurushii can mean breathlessness or distress depending on context. Shojo means manifestations of a condition, while hossa means an episode in which symptoms suddenly appear. When hearing terms such as cough, dizziness or numbness, report the person’s own words and what is known; vocabulary names alone do not establish disease.

Actual observation and responses follow the person’s condition, individual care plan and facility procedures. Communicate changes or risks to the necessary recipient, and do not try unfamiliar techniques from text alone.

kaigo-atomic-infection-chain.heading: The infection chain and protection suited to the task
paragraphs: Pathogens causing infection include bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Tell healthcare professionals about fever, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash, facial-color changes or other differences from usual. Symptoms alone do not identify the pathogen, and looking healthy does not establish freedom from infection risk.

Think in terms of the source, transmission route and receiving host. Materials containing pathogens can be sources; hands, objects, food and similar factors may form routes. Hosts include people and animals. Reducing sources, interrupting routes and supporting health have different purposes. Do not delay available precautions until all three kinds are ready.

The textbook gives norovirus and O157 as contact examples, influenza as a droplet example, and tuberculosis and measles as airborne examples. These classifications explain routes. Do not assume one precaution type is sufficient for one pathogen; confirm methods suited to the pathogen, task and current facility guidance.

Standard precautions are not only for people with a diagnosis. Consider task-related contact with blood, saliva, nasal secretions, vomit, urine, stool, damaged skin or mucous membranes. Select necessary gloves, masks, aprons or gowns and eye protection rather than applying one identical set to every task.

Gloves address hand-contact risks, aprons and similar items protect clothing from contamination, and goggles protect against eye splashes. Hats also appear in the textbook but are not always required for everyone. Wear masks covering nose, mouth and chin according to product instructions. Simply wearing one does not remove other precautions.

Change disposable gloves according to procedures when moving between people or care activities, or from dirty to clean work. Do not use one pair across several people. When removing them, fold contaminated surfaces inward, discard in the designated place and perform hand hygiene afterward. Gloves do not replace handwashing.

Communal living increases contact opportunities. Prevent bringing infection in, carrying it out and spreading it internally as distinct concerns. Combine hand hygiene, appropriate handling of supplies and surroundings, and staff coordination through facility procedures. People with reduced resistance need consideration, but healthy-looking people still require precautions.

This lesson checks infection mechanisms and judgments. Confirm protective-equipment use and removal, contaminated-material handling, and disinfectant products, concentrations and times through facility training and guidance. Do not invent new processing procedures or diagnoses from this text.

kaigo-atomic-hand-coverage.heading: Hand hygiene: commonly missed areas on both hands
paragraphs: Thorough rubbing of palms does not prove the backs, finger webs, thumbs, fingertips, nail areas and wrists were treated. Check both hands. Awareness of each area helps avoid finishing because foam is present while dirt remains.

For running water and liquid soap, consider the whole process: wetting, lathering and washing the required areas, thorough rinsing and drying with an appropriate paper towel or similar item. Areas covered by watches and rings are difficult to wash, so prepare beforehand according to facility rules. Washing around jewelry is not always sufficient.

Rub both palms over broad surfaces, then wash each hand’s back with the opposite palm. Interlace fingers to reach between them and attend to finger backs too. Check that you have not treated only the dominant hand.

Understand the textbook’s movements of enclosing and rotating each thumb in the opposite hand and treating fingertips and nail areas against the opposite palm. Switch hands and attend to wrists separately. Use the actual sequence and force practiced in facility training.

With a suitable hand-rub product, take the quantity specified by the manufacturer, distribute it over all areas and rub until dry. Cupping the hand helps receive liquid, but product instructions determine whether the amount is suitable. This method does not involve rinsing midway or wiping it off with paper.

For visible dirt, remove it with liquid soap and running water rather than relying on an alcohol product alone. Required methods may differ with pathogen and task, so check facility guidance. Do not treat handwashing and hand rubbing as identical acts that automatically substitute for one another.

Touching a contaminated surface afterward can dirty the hands again. Check locations and handling order for clean and used items. Knowing a diagram’s area sequence differs from proving that both hands were adequately treated. Confirm technique through direct training.

kaigo-atomic-body-mechanics.heading: Reduce back strain and support workers’ health
paragraphs: Body mechanics considers how bones, joints and muscles cooperate in movement. Assistance aims to protect the person and reduce workers’ exertion and back strain. One posture illustration cannot guarantee safe transfers for everyone.

The base of support is the area enclosed by the body’s supporting contact points. Relevant principles include suitably separating the feet and lowering the center of gravity. A correctly used cane adds a contact point and changes that area, but does not alone guarantee freedom from falls. Consider individual, equipment and floor conditions together.

Keeping the work close to the body and using large leg and buttock muscle groups helps avoid concentrating strain in the lower back. Avoid lifting a person with straight knees using the back alone, or twisting the waist while bearing weight. Reposition the feet to turn the body toward the direction of travel.

Other principles include gathering limbs within possible limits, moving the center of gravity horizontally, using whole-body movement, and considering a lever’s pivot and force direction. Distance from a pivot affects force, but knowledge alone does not determine which body part should be used as a pivot. Do not tie joints or bend into painful ranges to create a posture.

Do not reinterpret the material’s “pulling” as dragging skin against bedding or pulling an affected arm. Horizontal movement with friction-reducing equipment differs from directly dragging the body. Check skin, pain, abilities and equipment conditions.

Use the person’s abilities and consider lifts, sliding sheets, sliding boards and cooperation between trained staff. Adjusting posture does not authorize one worker to manually lift someone needing full transfer assistance. Prioritize checks of suitable equipment and methods rather than relying on manual lifting. Sheets and boards are different tools; similar names do not establish identical suitability or use.

Workers’ own food, nutrition, sleep, manageable exercise and rest matter too. Make time for meals and sleep and maintain daily rhythm. Do not carry anxiety alone; consult colleagues or senior staff and consider stress responses suited to you. Report illness or excessive strain, adjust support conditions and avoid continuing unreasonable work.

This section teaches principles and checks of working conditions. Transfers and repositioning require individual assessment, the care plan, equipment instructions and practical training. Do not try unfamiliar handling merely because you widened your stance or memorized principles.

kaigo-atomic-disaster.heading: Disaster preparation connects supplies, roles and contacts
paragraphs: Earthquakes, typhoons and fires pose different hazards. Regularly check the facility disaster plan, evacuation routes, communication methods and community cooperation. Share who will help whom in advance rather than assigning roles for the first time during a disaster.

Possible supplies include water and food, personal medicines and medical supplies, first-aid items, lighting, a radio and batteries, warmth supplies, clothing, hygiene items and head protection. Check preparations for valuables such as cash and necessary documents according to personal needs and facility management. These are organizing examples, not one identical quantity or complete list for everyone. Check the plan, expiry dates and actual needs; the textbook picture is not an exhaustive inventory.

Drills check support if the usual route is unavailable, designated helpers for people needing mobility assistance and alternative communication if contact fails. Record the locations, people and conditions actually checked. Packing supplies into a bag differs from completing evacuation.

For people using powered medical devices such as oxygen concentrators, consult healthcare professionals and equipment staff beforehand about who contacts whom during an outage and how necessary support, backup equipment or power will be secured. Prepare according to the actual device and plan. This lesson does not ask workers to determine connections or oxygen flow.

[Learning example] A supply list exists, but no outage helper has been designated for a person receiving oxygen therapy. The list alone does not complete preparation. Confirm responsibilities, contacts, equipment needs and movement plans with relevant people. Having equipment differs from having an arrangement that can actually use it.

kaigo-atomic-communication.heading: Two-way communication and choosing questions
paragraphs: Communication exchanges thoughts, feelings and information and checks understanding. Speaker and listener roles alternate; both convey and receive. Staff finishing everything they wanted to say does not prove the other person understood.

Speech, writing and sign language use language. Do not equate sign language with unrestricted gestures. Facial expressions, posture, gaze and gestures provide nonverbal clues. Check these as well as words in ways suited to the person.

Active listening means listening attentively and accurately; empathy means trying to understand feelings from the other person’s position; acceptance means receiving their feelings and opinions. Although related, these have different purposes. None means making the person conform to the conclusion staff think correct.

Closed questions, answered with yes/no or limited choices, help specific checks. Open questions invite broader expression of thoughts or wishes. However, only using closed questions may become one-sided, while repeatedly asking “why” even in open questions can feel accusatory. Select questions according to purpose and burden.

Values relate to the era and surroundings in which people grew up and their experiences. Respect feelings and thinking and speak courteously as adults. Check meanings within the necessary scope with family and other professionals as well as the person, supporting trustworthy care.

[Learning example] Repeatedly asking someone who does not want to attend an event “Why aren’t you going?” is not automatically good because the question is open. Pause questioning, listen to what they want to say and, if needed, use a brief check to clarify choice. Question form alone does not guarantee a good exchange.

kaigo-atomic-listening-consent.heading: From listening to explanation, understanding and consent
paragraphs: Repeating the main points of the person’s words shows listening and checks misunderstandings. Preserve timing, body location and how they felt rather than replacing their account with a staff conclusion. Do not communicate “since yesterday” as something that started today.

Face the person and adjust eye level, speaking pace, a calm voice and pauses. Crossed arms or drawing far away can suggest not listening. However, gaze and gesture meanings differ by person and culture; do not impose one eye contact pattern or posture on everyone.

Conversational distance and physical touch are interpreted differently according to the person, situation, manner, force and frequency. Do not assume holding a hand conveys warmth to everyone. Check the interaction the person wants; general cultural tendencies cannot substitute for personal wishes.

Present assistance options and explain each benefit and disadvantage in a way the person can understand. Support thinking, choosing and expressing a decision, and respect it. Merely stating the purpose does not establish consent.

[Learning example] The person nods before disadvantages have been explained, and staff intend to record full understanding and consent. Do not treat a nod alone as proof of complete understanding. Provide the missing information and check understanding and the actual choice. Link consent to the scope of assistance explained.
This lesson practices communication and checking. Actual assistance follows the person’s condition, plan and facility procedures. Do not record unconfirmed consent or unperformed support as complete.

120.title: Observe risks and share near misses
objectives: Separate words, observations and measurements and record risks and unconfirmed causes.
Share injury-free near misses, using terms accurately to support prevention.
120.context: Learn to report observed risks and causes that are still unknown. The vocabulary list is a reference, not a requirement to learn every term anew in one sitting.
120.artCaption: Staff review events together. Share incidents without injuries too, and report causes only to the extent confirmed.

121.title: The infection chain and protection suited to the task
objectives: Distinguish sources, routes and hosts and explain necessary precautions before diagnosis.
Choose protection according to task risks and distinguish glove changes from hand hygiene.
121.context: This knowledge lesson checks infection routes and equipment selection. It does not involve practical processing or mixing disinfectant.
121.artCaption: Staff check protection suited to the task. Items in the illustration are not one identical set for every activity.

122.title: Hand hygiene: commonly missed areas on both hands
objectives: Distinguish water-and-soap washing from hand rubbing and check areas of both hands.
Explain product- and facility-appropriate hygiene considering visible dirt and recontact.
122.context: Check differences in areas and methods. Reading movement descriptions does not replace practical facility training.
122.artCaption: Staff wash under running water. The image alone cannot establish washing of all areas, rinsing and drying.

123.title: Reduce back strain and support workers’ health
objectives: Distinguish base-of-support, center-of-gravity, muscle and lever principles from permission to perform techniques.
Reduce strain through abilities, equipment, staffing and workers’ physical and mental health.
123.context: This knowledge lesson combines support conditions instead of relying on posture alone. It involves no practice of manually lifting a person.
123.artCaption: Staff check working conditions around an empty bed. This does not demonstrate lifting methods or practical safety.

124.title: Disaster preparation connects supplies, roles and contacts
objectives: Check disaster-specific hazards, supplies, roles and communication beforehand.
Connect individual medical-device needs to plans and distinguish preparation from completed evacuation.
124.context: Check responsibilities and individual needs rather than judging preparation from supply numbers alone. No equipment operation or oxygen-setting changes are performed.
124.artCaption: The scene includes rest, consultation and preparation of disaster supplies. It does not establish individual assignments or completed evacuation.

125.title: Two-way communication and choosing questions
objectives: Distinguish verbal/nonverbal communication, active listening, empathy and acceptance, and check mutual understanding.
Choose open or closed questions according to purpose and personal burden.
125.context: Learn two-way understanding of what the person wants to convey rather than simply continuing questions.
125.artCaption: Listen and check meaning. Question form alone does not establish understanding.

126.title: From listening to explanation, understanding and consent
objectives: Adapt repetition, eye level, pauses and distance to the person and accurately check what was heard.
Explain benefits and disadvantages and distinguish nodding from understanding, decision-making and consent.
126.context: Distinguish what was said from what the person understood and chose, and check assistance scope.
126.artCaption: Explain object locations or assistance. Understanding and consent require separate checking beyond speaking alone.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-risk-observatio.prompt: A wheelchair moved, but the person did not fall and has no injury. How should this near miss be handled?
options: Record movement and confirmed conditions and separately share unknown causes.
With no injury, omit observation and records.
Record the brakes as the established cause before inspection.
Wait for an injury in a later accident before discussing precautions.
rationales: Share established facts from injury-free events to help prevent recurrence.
Near misses contain useful prevention information; no injury does not justify omission.
An assumption before inspection cannot be recorded as a confirmed cause.
Consider prevention from this hazard rather than waiting for harm.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-infection-chain.prompt: A task involves touching vomit from someone without an infection diagnosis yet. Which approach is appropriate?
options: No diagnosis permits bare-hand contact.
A healthy appearance permits omission of protection and hand hygiene.
Use protection and hand hygiene suited to contact risks according to procedures without waiting for diagnosis.
Gloves remove the need for hand hygiene afterward.
rationales: Standard precautions consider vomit-contact risks rather than diagnosis alone.
Healthy appearance does not justify omitting required precautions.
Check task-appropriate equipment and methods and take necessary precautions before diagnosis too.
Gloves and subsequent hand hygiene are both needed.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-hand-coverage.prompt: Both palms were washed, but thumbs and nail areas have not been reached. What is appropriate?
options: Enough foam means unwashed areas count as washed.
Treat required areas of both hands using the chosen method before finishing.
One clean palm means the other hand is complete too.
Memorizing the diagram order removes the need to check actual areas.
rationales: Foam quantity alone does not prove coverage of every area.
This checks needed areas on both sides, including thumbs, fingertips and nail surrounds.
Check each hand and area separately.
Knowing the procedure differs from adequately performing it.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-body-mechanics.prompt: A care worker stands with feet apart. Does that alone authorize lifting every person without help?
options: A wide stance removes checks of personal condition.
A lower center of gravity removes equipment needs.
Understanding a posture image permits transfers without practical training.
No. Check abilities, equipment, staffing and trained methods as well as posture.
rationales: Foot width cannot replace assessment of the person’s condition and abilities.
Posture adjustments do not remove consideration of suitable assistive equipment.
Understanding an image alone does not establish safe practical transfer ability.
This checks working conditions, including equipment and methods, rather than relying only on principles.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-disaster.prompt: Disaster supplies are ready, but nobody is assigned to support an oxygen-therapy user during an outage. What is appropriate?
options: A supply list completes individual responsibility checks too.
Look for contact details for the first time when power fails.
Confirm roles, contacts, required backup and movement plans with healthcare professionals and equipment staff.
The worker assembling supplies independently decides oxygen settings.
rationales: Supplies and the person’s required support arrangements are separate checks.
Advance roles and communication checks reduce confusion.
This confirms an individual plan suited to the person and device with relevant people.
The lesson or supply preparation does not authorize independent medical-device settings.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-communication.prompt: Someone is repeatedly asking “Why aren’t you going?” about an event the person does not want to attend. Which review is appropriate?
options: Stop the interrogating approach, listen to what the person wants to say and check wishes with questions suited to their burden.
Continue the same question without a response because it is open.
Avoid every specific check because all closed questions are bad.
Treat staff ideas as the person’s wishes.
rationales: An open form alone does not make communication good; check burden and wishes.
Repeated “why” questions can feel accusatory and need adjustment.
Closed questions can clarify choices or facts.
Staff decisions must not replace listening to the person.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-listening-conse.prompt: The person nods before disadvantages have been explained, and staff intend to record full understanding and consent. What is appropriate?
options: Nodding allows the remaining explanation to be skipped.
Stating the purpose means consent to all assistance.
Later record even unexplained content as agreed.
Explain benefits and disadvantages understandably and check understanding and the person’s choice.
rationales: A nod does not show understanding of content not yet explained.
Explanation, consent and its scope each need checking.
Do not invent consent to unexplained content as a recorded fact.
Provide necessary information and support understanding and expression of a decision.
